newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Complaints dog Nigerian voter registration.
newsitem.headline: Complaints dog Nigerian voter registration.

text.p: A 10-day registration of Nigerians to vote in elections to end military rule was ending on Wednesday amid complaints of some fraud and insufficient materials to process applicants.
"I am an aspirant to vote and I have been coming here since last week but there are no cards to register me," a potential voter in the capital Abuja said on state television NTA.

NTA prime time news on Tuesday showed many places where registration officers sat without cards to issue to potential voters. Nigeria had expected to register half the 100 million people in Africas most populous nation.
Political observers said voter registration was crucial to General Sani Abachas plan to transfer power to a democratically-elected president on October 1, 1998.
Nigeria is shunned worldwide for alleged human rights violations and a lack of democracy.

It was suspended from the Commonwealth, which groups Britain and its former colonies, for hanging nine minority rights activists in 1995, including author Ken Saro-Wiwa. The Commonwealth gave Nigeria until this year to restore democracy but military rulers are following their own schedule.
After registration began last week, some political parties complained of people registering twice in order to rig forthcoming elections.

But NECON said the alleged fraud would not affect elections. "If there are objections they can be raised when the voters lists are displayed and this will be rectified," said NECON administrative secretary for Lagos state Ademola Johnson.
Some state military administrators have warned that people will have to show a voters card to receive salaries or state facilities, but NECON distanced itself from that tactic to spur registration.
"It has not been 100 percent perfect but to a reasonable level I think it is satisfactory," Gambo Lawal, chairman of the centrist Grassroots Democratic Party, said of the voter registration.

Many in Lagos appeared to be making a last effort to register, with witnesses reporting several registration centres in the country's biggest city were full. In several states, work was to end at noon Wednesday to give time to register.
"I was able to finally register but it took quite a while," said Ibrahim Imogui, who turned 18 last year and will be voting for the first time.

Nigerias last attempt at democracy ended in chaos when the previous military ruler annulled a presidential vote in 1993. Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll is in detention along with many other opposition figures.

Abacha seized power after the annulment and has promised to hand over to an elected president on October 1, 1998. Critics are wary that Abacha may try to succeed himself and point to a recent interview in which he did not rule out contesting next years presidential election.
